terms.grammar: ablative of the way with the adverb sūrsum or deorsum; often with hāc, “this way”
evidence: Ter. Ad. 573: porticum apud macellum hāc deorsum
terms.comment: In Terence’s scene of directions the slave Syrus sends Demea “down this way” to the colonnade by the market, and then “straight up the street”. As in English, up and down need not mean a slope: they say which way along the street. Of a place a little way along (“the shop just up the street”), say paulō ultrā, or hīc in proximō of a door or two away.

evidence: Ter. Ad. 582: ad sinistram hāc rēctā platēā

phrases.latin: Nōstin' porticum apud macellum hāc deorsum?
phrases.english: Do you know the colonnade by the market, down this way?

phrases.latin: ubi eās praeterieris, ad sinistram hāc rēctā platēā
phrases.english: when you’ve gone past the house, turn left, straight along this street

phrases.latin: Hāc platēā sūrsum ambulābimus ūsque ad fontem.
phrases.english: We’ll walk up the street as far as the fountain.

phrases.latin: Pistrīna est paulō ultrā, in eādem viā.
phrases.english: The bakery is just up the street.
